**Summary.** Luthier v7 already measures stress on the beat, line endings and vowels on held notes, but it set aside a rule for a word's pitch shape and any vowel table for men, and its songs put weak syllables on the downbeat. In 199 Billboard songs and 80 Rolling Stone 200 songs, weak syllables take beat 1 only 4% to 6% of the time, and a word's stressed syllable is lower than its other syllables in 18% to 20% of words. Songs 54 and 55 do both about twice as often (10% to 12%, and 34%), mostly through line openings like "And" and "But" on the bar line. On vowels, height alone barely matters; held high notes do, with men's held top notes open 61% of the time and reduced only 7%. v8 should grade its stress cost, give weak line openings a pickup, add a word-shape rule for pitch, and add a vowel rule for held high notes by voice, all as weights in Part 21's placement.

## What Luthier v7 does now

v7 is already strong on words: it measured stress, vowels and line endings on large corpora and built them in. Its gaps are the ones it named itself: no rule for a word's pitch shape, nothing that keeps weak syllables off the downbeat beyond the stress floor, and no vowel table for men.

What it has (Luthier v7):

- **Stress on the beat (Window 25).** On 646,345 karaoke syllables, a syllable on a strong beat is stressed 75% of the time against a base rate of 54%. The engine's alignment floor reads stressed syllables on beats, with monosyllabic function words counted unstressed.

- **Anticipation credited (Module 10.19, Window 69).** A stressed syllable an eighth before an empty strong beat counts as on it (rock does this with about a quarter of its stresses).

- **Length.** Stressed syllables are only a tenth longer; the title's last stress is held about 1.5 times; a line's last note runs about 1.9 times the rest, and a line that ends short is named. English popular song holds a word's last syllable rather than its stressed one (Window 98).

- **The high note.** The line peaks early (17% of the way in) and its last stress is held low; the peak avoids reduced vowels.

- **Vowels (Window 39).** Register does not change the vowel in pop; held notes favour open vowels (56% against 50%), the strongest phonetic hit signal v7 found. A vowel term rewards open vowels on held notes and forbids a reduced vowel on the peak. Lax vowels lean to short notes, tense vowels and diphthongs to long ones (a lean, named per note).

- **Intelligibility (Window 69).** Word familiarity is the one large effect; stress mismatch and melisma are small; consonant and mishearing loads are reported. Female vowel bands by pitch (trouble from C5) are carried as information.

- **Entries (fixes 731, 742, 749).** The kept line is drawn by its first syllable's stress; unstressed openings still land on the bar line three or four times as often as in kept songs.

What v7 did not build, in its own words: a pitch-accent rule, male or belt vowel tables, and isochrony. Its reasons were that no English corpus coded accents against melody and the proxies were modest. Two corpora now let both be measured directly (below).

Where songs 54 to 56 struggled with words: two syllables on one onset (749.1, 749.26), placement deaths at long lines (749.3, 749.25, 749.30), and unstressed openings on the bar line (742, 749). Part 21 traced the placement deaths to slots fixed in bars; this study looks at the syllables themselves.

## Stress and the beat: what the research says

The text-setting literature treats stress placement as a ranked set of preferences, not a pass-or-fail rule, and it adds two things v7 lacks: stress has levels (inside a word, across words, at phrase ends), and weak syllables on strong beats are worse than strong syllables off them.

- **Halle and Lerdahl, then Hayes.** Halle and Lerdahl (1993) gave the first explicit model of how speakers fit new words to a tune; Hayes recasts it as constraint conflict, where a good setting is the best compromise among stressed syllables on strong positions, no long gaps without a syllable, no extreme crowding, and phrase breaks at line ends, and a stress may move to a weak position to avoid a long gap [(Hayes, Textsetting as Constraint Conflict](https://brucehayes.org/Textsetting)). Part 21 already recommends this weighted approach for placement.

- **Stress has levels** [(Hayes and Kaun 1996,](https://www.brucehayes.org/papers/HayesAndKaunMetrics1996.pdf) 670 folk-song lines set by ten speakers): Word-internal stress falls are set more strictly than those across words.

   - Phrase ends are set more strictly the bigger the phrase: at the end of an intonational phrase, 1,102 settings matched the metre against 12 that did not. Unfilled positions count as weaker than any unstressed syllable.

   - Inversions (a stress on a weak position) are a last resort and cluster at line ends. Syllables tend to get beats in proportion to their natural length; a long first syllable is not crowded.

- **Natural length in pop.** Ryan (2022), on 2,371 English popular songs, found placement on the grid is sensitive to a syllable's natural duration even after final lengthening is controlled, measured between perceptual centres [(English Language & Linguistics](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/english-language-and-linguistics/article/abs/syllable-weight-and-natural-duration-in-textsetting-popular-music-in-english/50F8885341914C37D6F1BD22A632A0B6)).

- **Short stressed syllables and the snap.** Temperley and Temperley (2011) tie the Scotch snap (a sixteenth on the beat, then a dotted eighth) to English's very short stressed syllables; four vowels account for much of both [(Music Perception)](https://artboulevard.org/items/330539/).

- **Composers align better than after-the-fact setters.** Palmer and Kelly (1992) found syllables aligned with linguistic or musical accent are sung longer, and compound and phrase stress follow English's rules [(PDF](https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Palmer1992.pdf)).

- **Stopwords.** In 679 popular lead sheets, monosyllabic function words become less likely the stronger the metric position, and unstressed syllables are very unlikely on downbeats ([Nichols et al. 2009)](https://archives.ismir.net/ismir2009/paper/000084.pdf).

For v8 this means the alignment check should be graded: a word-internal mismatch costs more than one across words; a weak syllable on beat 1 costs more than a stress on an offbeat; a line's end is strict and its start free.

## Stress and pitch: what the research says

In English, pitch is a stronger cue to stress than length, and songs follow speech here: stressed syllables tend to sit higher than their neighbours. The studies are small, which is why v7 left it out; the corpus below measures it directly.

- **Chen and Mok (2014)** , 15 English songs, multi-syllable words only [(Speech Prosody)](https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/lin/people/peggy/ChenMok_SP2014.pdf): Lexical stress matched the metre perfectly in about 68% of cases, a secondary match in 9%, a mismatch in 23%.

   - Judged against the notes either side, primary stresses matched the pitch pattern (higher than the neighbours) 141 times against 92, about 1.5 to 1; for duration the ratio was 1.2.

   - They conclude pitch matches stress better than duration does, as pitch is the stronger cue to English stress in speech.

- **Nichols et al. (2009)** , 679 lead sheets: stressed syllables and melodic peaks are associated, and peaks are more often on content words than function words, though the paper reports this only in figures ([ISMIR)](https://archives.ismir.net/ismir2009/paper/000084.pdf).

- **Across languages.** A comparison of Turkish and English children's songs coded stress against metrical strength and melodic peaks, building on the English findings that stressed syllables align with higher notes [(Kabak and Domene Moreno)](https://glowlinguistics.org/42/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2019/03/glow_oslo_2019_with_names.pdf).

- **Speech's own pattern.** In English, pitch accents fall on stressed syllables, which are also longer, louder and have fuller vowels [(Zahner, Kember and Braun 2017](https://ling.uni-konstanz.de/securedl/sdl-eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJpYXQiOjE3MzA1NzQ4MzUsImV4cCI6MTczMTI2NjAzNSwidXNlciI6MCwiZ3JvdXBzIjpbMCwtMV0sImZpbGUiOiJmaWxlYWRtaW4vbGluZy9hZy1icmF1bi16aW5uL0NvbmZlcmVuY2VfUGFwZXJzL0ludGVyc3BlZWNoMjAxN19NdXNpY2FsX1phaG5lcktlbWJlckJyYXVuLnBkZiIsInBhZ2UiOjk5MzQwfQ.CTB2a5yyhXRv-cR4pT0MVC5blbB8rVEC7hzllBZv3G8/Interspeech2017_Musical_ZahnerKemberBraun.pdf)).

The simplest test of a pitch-accent rule is inside the word, where nothing else changes: is the stressed syllable of "mother" or "believe" higher than the other one? That is what the corpus measure below does.

## Vowels and high notes: what the research says

Vowels lose their identity as the sung pitch climbs toward the vowel's first resonance, and singers answer by adjusting the vowel rather than avoiding it. For men in pop the critical zone is the top of the chest voice, about E4 to A4, where belters tune a resonance to the second harmonic.

- **Where identification fails.** Above about C5 (523 Hz), listeners' identification of every vowel but /a/ falls toward chance ([Friedrichs et al.](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10142399/1/Friedrichs_Manuscript_Revised_v2.pdf)). Smith and Scott (1980) found isolated soprano vowels above F5 lost half their intelligibility against C♯5, but with a raised larynx, as in popular styles, the drop between C♯5 and F5 was only 10% [(Collister and Huron 2008](https://d-scholarship.pitt.edu/19444/1/EMR000050a%2DCollister%2DHuron.pdf)).

- **Men too, at their own pitches.** Chan and Kuang (JASA) played words sung by a soprano, mezzo, tenor and baritone from C2 to D6 to 102 listeners: identification declines as the fundamental approaches the first formant, sung vowels decline earlier than synthesized ones, AE and EH are easily confused, and IY is not safe when sung [(summary)](https://synapsesocial.com/papers/W7160911134). Its cause is both the singers' adjustments and the spectrum itself.

- **What male belters do.** Six male music-theatre singers, recorded on [e] and [ɔ] at the top of their belt range (about 250 to 440 Hz, roughly B3 to A4), tuned the first resonance to the second harmonic in every quality ([Bourne et al. 2016)](https://isidore.science/document/10670/1.ih8oq6). Titze's belt examples modify toward /æ/, /a/ and a bright rounded vowel in the G4 to C5 range, and his instructor did not count /i/ as a belt vowel ([Titze)](https://vocology.utah.edu/_resources/documents/formant_frequency_shifts_titze.pdf).

- **Belt against opera.** Titze and Worley model belting as vowels shaped like a megaphone, keeping the fundamental and second harmonic below the first formant, where operatic singing lifts the harmonics over it ([JASA 2009](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2757425)).

- **Modification is the norm.** Pedagogy describes shading vowels so the sung pitch or a harmonic sits near a formant, varying with voice size, note length, loudness and approach ([Nix 2004](https://ncvs.org/archive/pas/2004/abstracts/nix1.htm)).

Two things follow for the engine. A vowel rule for men belongs at the top of the singer's chest range and on held notes there, not at a fixed absolute pitch. And close vowels (/i/, /u/) are the risky ones on a held high note, while open and mid vowels are the ones belters can tune.

## What the songs do: measured

In real songs a weak syllable almost never takes beat 1 and a word's stressed syllable is rarely its lowest note; songs 54 and 55 break both about twice as often. On vowels, men's songs lean to open vowels and away from reduced ones on held high notes, not on high notes as such.

![Songs 54 and 55 put weak syllables on beat 1 two to three times as often as hits do](data:image/png;base64,)

*Source: studies/words/words_test.py on CoCoPops Billboard (stress from the CMU dictionary) and Rolling Stone 200 (stress from its own spine), and the lead sheets of songs 54 and 55*

The method: `studies/words/words_test.py` reads every sung syllable of the 4/4 songs in two corpora, with its note, its place in the bar and its word. Billboard (199 songs in 4/4) has lyrics but no stress, so stress comes from the CMU dictionary, with one-syllable function words counted unstressed as v7 does. The Rolling Stone 200 subset (80 songs) carries its own stress marks, from Tan, Lustig and Temperley's algorithm, and agrees with Billboard on every measure both can make (lines and vowels are read from Billboard only). Songs 54 and 55 are read from their lead sheets the same way; they have only 44 and 41 words of two or more syllables, so their word-pitch figures are rough.

- **Stress and the beat.** Stressed syllables take beat 1 19% of the time and beat 3 16%; unstressed syllables take beat 1 4% and beat 3 5% (Billboard; Rolling Stone 21% and 16% against 6% and 5%). Of one-syllable function words, 5% fall on beat 1, against 18% of one-syllable content words. Songs 54 and 55 put 12% and 10% of their weak syllables on beat 1, about two and a half times the corpus, and as many function words there as content words. Most are line openings ("And", "But", "I", "To" on the bar line), the entry problem of fixes 742 and 749, and the rest are articles mid-line.

- **Stress and pitch, inside the word.** In 6,380 Billboard words with a primary stress and an unstressed syllable, the stressed syllable is higher 44% of the time, level 36% and lower 20% (Rolling Stone 45%, 37%, 18%). Words that start on their stress are lower only 18% of the time; words stressed later ("believe") 27%. Songs 54 and 55 sing the stress lower 34% of the time.

- **Local peaks.** A stressed syllable is a local peak (above both neighbours) 19% of the time, an unstressed one 9%, about two to one in both corpora. Song 55's weak syllables are peaks 19% of the time, as often as its stressed ones.

- **Stress and length inside the word.** The stressed syllable is longer than the word's unstressed syllables 30% of the time and shorter 19%; half are the same length. Song 55 sings it shorter 37% of the time.

- **The line's last stress** (3,569 Billboard lines with three stresses or more):

   - It lands on beat 1 or 3 only 21% of the time against 37% for the line's other stresses, and on an offbeat eighth 47% of the time: it anticipates.

   - It is longer than the line's mean note 65% of the time (other stresses 42%), and above the line's mean pitch only 46% (others 57%): held and low, as Window 25 found.

   - It is the rhyme word two times in three.

- **Vowels by register and length, by singer** (Billboard, 94 male and 28 female singers by SingerSex.txt; male median note D4, median top note A4):

| Notes | Men: open | Men: close | Men: reduced | Women: open | Women: close | Women: reduced |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| All sung notes | 48% | 30% | 22% | 49% | 32% | 19% |
| Top tenth of the song's range | 50% | 32% | 18% | 52% | 34% | 14% |
| At or above E4 (men) / C5 (women) | 49% | 32% | 19% | 51% | 39% | 10% |
| Held a beat or more | 59% | 30% | 11% | 56% | 36% | 9% |
| Held and in the top tenth | 61% | 32% | 7% | 55% | 38% | 8% |

Height alone barely moves the vowel, as v7's Window 39 found; length does, and length at the top does most. Men's held high notes carry an open vowel 61% of the time and a reduced one 7%, a third of the base rate. Close vowels do not thin out at the top for either sex: singers modify them rather than avoid them, as the acoustics studies describe.

## What v8 should do

Keep v7's word rules and add three: a graded cost for weak syllables on strong beats, a word-shape rule for pitch, and a vowel rule for held high notes by voice. Each fits Part 21's weighted placement, where a setting is the best compromise rather than a pass or a death.

1. **Grade the stress cost** (Hayes and Kaun; Hayes's constraints):

   - a weak syllable on beat 1 costs most, on beat 3 next; a stress on an offbeat costs little, and nothing when it anticipates an empty beat (10.19 stands); a mismatch inside a word costs more than one across words; a line's end is strict and its start free.

2. **Weak line openings take a pickup.** An unstressed first syllable ("And", "But", "I", "To", "a") goes before the bar line, or the line starts on its first stress. This is 742 and 749's fix, now with a band: weak syllables on beat 1 at most about 6% of weak syllables (corpus 4% to 6%; songs 54 and 55, 10% to 12%), and one-syllable function words on beat 1 at most about 6% of them.

3. **A word-shape rule for pitch** (the pitch-accent rule v7 left out): in a word of two or more syllables, the stressed syllable is at or above the word's other syllables. Target: lower at most about 20% of such words (corpus 18% to 20%; songs 54 and 55, 34%), and a weak syllable a local peak at most about 10% of the time, about half the rate of stressed syllables.

4. **Inside the word, the stress is not the shortest.** Stressed syllables shorter than the word's weak syllables at most about 20% of the time (corpus 19%; song 55, 37%). v7's finding that stressed syllables are only slightly longer overall stands; this is a floor inside the word, not a lengthening rule.

5. **The line's last stress.** Let it anticipate (about half land on an offbeat eighth), hold it (about two lines in three it is longer than the line's mean note), keep it at or below the line's middle pitch, and prefer it on the rhyme word. Most of this is v7's already; the anticipation of the last stress is new.

6. **A vowel rule by voice and length.** On notes held a beat or more in the top tenth of the singer's range: open vowels at least about 55% and reduced vowels at most about 10% (men 61% and 7%, women 55% and 8%). No rule for height alone. Close vowels (IY, UW) on such notes are allowed, as singers sing them, but the songbook flags each one for the singer to open slightly. For a baritone that zone starts around D4 to E4; for a tenor, around G4 to A4.

7. **Natural length.** A long syllable (a tense vowel or diphthong, or a heavy closed syllable) is not crowded onto a sixteenth; v7's vowel-duration lean becomes part of the placement score (Ryan; Hayes and Kaun).

Checks for the port:

- Rerun songs 54 and 55 and compare with the corpus bands above: weak syllables and function words on beat 1, word-internal pitch and length, weak-syllable peaks, vowels on held high notes.

- The corpus checks reproduce from `studies/words/words_results.json`.

- No placement death from the new costs: they weigh, they do not forbid (Part 21).

## Files and sources

In the repo, `studies/words/`:

- `parse_words.py`: every sung syllable of CoCoPops Billboard and the Rolling Stone 200 files with stress, with its note, place in the bar, length, section and line start.

- `words_test.py`: the measures in this report, for the corpora and for songs 54 and 55.

- `words_results.json`: every figure in this report. `sung_syllables.json` is not committed; the parser rebuilds it.

Data: [CoCoPops](https://github.com/Computational-Cognitive-Musicology-Lab/CoCoPops), CC BY-NC 4.0, derived counts only; stress from the CMU Pronouncing Dictionary (via the `pronouncing` package) for Billboard. Luthier v7 Windows 25, 39, 69 and 98 and Module 10.19 for what the engine already does.
